title: What are Arrays.parallelSort, Arrays.parallelPrefix and Arrays.parallelSetAll? How do they use the common ForkJoinPool, and when does parallel sorting actually pay off?
keyPoints: Arrays.parallelSort splits the array, sorts chunks on different threads, and merges the results.
Arrays.parallelPrefix computes a running cumulative operation (prefix scan) in parallel.
Arrays.parallelSetAll fills each element from its index using a generator function in parallel.
All three use the common ForkJoinPool (shared process-wide, default size = processors - 1).
They fall back to sequential execution below an internal threshold (about 8192 for parallelSort).
Parallel pays off only for large arrays on multi-core machines; benchmark before choosing.
Do not mix blocking I/O into anything sharing the common pool.

s1_definition.oneliner: Arrays.parallelSort, parallelPrefix and parallelSetAll offload large array work to the common ForkJoinPool, but they only beat the sequential versions when the array is large and the machine has multiple cores.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **`parallelSort`** – parallel merge sort; splits, sorts chunks on threads, merges; sequential below ~8192 elements.
- **`parallelPrefix`** – running cumulative operation (prefix scan) in parallel across the array.
- **`parallelSetAll`** – fills each element from its index using a generator function in parallel.
- **Common ForkJoinPool** – shared process-wide, default parallelism = available processors minus 1.
- **Threshold** – all three fall back to sequential for small arrays; parallel overhead > work saved.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must sort a million transactions, compute a running balance, and fill in a fee schedule. One clerk sorting the pile is slow; several clerks each sort a stack and merge. ParallelPrefix is like computing the running day-end balance down the ledger. ParallelSetAll is like many clerks each filling a different row. But for twenty transactions, one clerk is faster than organizing a team.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  parallelSort:
  [unsorted array, 1M elements]
       │
       ▼
  Split into chunks (~8K each)
  ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐ ┌────────┐
  │ Sort   │ │ Sort   │ │ Sort   │  worker threads
  └────┬───┘ └────┬───┘ └────┬───┘
       └────merge─┴──merge───┘
                  │
           [sorted array]

  parallelPrefix (add):
  Input:  [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
  Output: [10, 30, 60, 100, 150]  (running sum)

  parallelSetAll:
  fees[i] = baseFee + i * step  (computed in parallel per index)

  All use: ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Arrays.parallelSort, parallelPrefix, and parallelSetAll do array work in parallel on the common ForkJoinPool. ParallelSort is a parallel merge sort. ParallelPrefix computes a running scan. ParallelSetAll fills from an index generator. All three fall back to sequential below an internal threshold.

They share the common pool with parallel streams, so do not mix blocking I/O. And they only beat sequential for large arrays on multi-core machines.

Remember one sentence: these parallel array methods offload large CPU-bound work to the common ForkJoinPool and only pay off when the array is large and there are spare cores.
